Sampling within a region

Source: R/design-spatial.R
design_spatial.Rd

Draws a simple random sample of the rows whose coordinates fall inside a region. It decides where sampling happens, not how evenly it covers the ground: for a sample spread evenly across space — usually far more precise when what you measure varies smoothly — use design_spread(), on the frame restricted to the region if need be.

Usage

design_spatial(coords, region, n, crs = 4326, na_rm = FALSE)

Arguments

coords

Two column names, c(x, y) with longitude first, or the name of one POINT geometry column. See "Coordinate order".

region

An sf or sfc geometry of POLYGON or MULTIPOLYGON features, or a list of them. A row inside any of them is inside the region. Each is reprojected to the coordinates' CRS when its own differs.

n

Number of rows to draw from inside the region, or a plan from plan_size().

crs

Coordinate reference system of the coordinate columns. Defaults to EPSG:4326. A geometry column named in coords keeps its own CRS when it has one.

na_rm

Drop rows with missing coordinates instead of raising an error.

Value

A design object, for use with draw().

Coordinate order

coords is c(x, y) — longitude first, then latitude — matching sf::st_as_sf(). Getting this backwards puts your points somewhere else entirely, so it is worth checking against a known landmark once. When the coordinates are longitude and latitude, a latitude outside -90 to 90 or a longitude outside -180 to 360 is refused, since it means the columns are the wrong way round or hold projected coordinates.

A POINT geometry column, such as the geometry of an sf frame, can stand in for the two columns: name it alone, as in coords = "geometry", and each row's position is read with sf::st_coordinates(). The column's own CRS is used when it has one, and region is reprojected to it.

Edges of a longitude/latitude region

With spherical geometry (sf::sf_use_s2(), the default), each edge of a longitude/latitude region follows the great circle between its two corners, the shortest path on the globe. On a flat longitude/latitude map that path bows towards the nearer pole wherever the edge runs east-west away from the equator; edges along a meridian or the equator do not bow. A wide box is therefore a different shape from the rectangle it looks like on such a map. The top edge of a box from -50 to 50 degrees of longitude and -30 to 30 of latitude reaches latitude 41.9 at longitude 0, so a row at (0, 41) is inside it, and its bottom edge reaches -41.9. A box from -5 to 5 degrees of longitude and 40 to 50 of latitude takes in a row at (0, 50.05) and leaves out one at (0, 40.05).

draw(), inclusion_prob(), joint_prob() and plot() warn, with class drawn_geodesic_edges, when an edge of region passes more than 0.1 degrees (about 11 km) from the straight line between its corners on a longitude/latitude map. To make the edges follow those straight lines, add vertices along them in degree space before you build the design:

flat <- sf::st_set_crs(region, NA)    # coordinates as plain numbers
flat <- sf::st_segmentize(flat, 0.1)  # a vertex at least every 0.1 degrees
region <- sf::st_set_crs(flat, 4326)

An edge 0.1 degrees long bows by about a metre at most. The CRS has to come off for the middle step: on a region that keeps it, sf::st_segmentize() needs the lwgeom package and places the new vertices along the great circles, under either s2 setting, and the bow stays. A region larger than a hemisphere needs splitting first; see the next section.

Regions that cross the antimeridian

With spherical geometry enabled (sf::sf_use_s2(), the default), consecutive polygon vertices are joined by the shortest great-circle path. An edge from longitude -179 to +179 therefore spans the 2 degrees across the antimeridian, not the 358 degrees the coordinates suggest. A "whole world" rectangle collapses into a 2-degree-wide pole-to-pole strip of 2.8 million km2 – against the roughly 510 million km2 of the globe – and contains almost nothing.

Ring orientation is not the cause and reversing it does not help: sf normalises winding, so both directions give the same strip. Adding vertices along the edges in degree space, as in the previous section, does not rescue a region this large either. s2 takes the smaller of the two areas a ring divides the globe into as its inside, so a ring around more than half the globe encloses the rest of the globe instead.

The short way is the right reading for a region meant to cross the antimeridian, such as a box from longitude 179 to -179. draw(), inclusion_prob(), joint_prob() and plot() warn, with class drawn_antimeridian, whenever an edge of region joins two longitudes more than 180 degrees apart, and the warning gives both readings. An edge from -180 to 180 is one of them: both ends lie on the same meridian, so under spherical geometry the edge spans no longitude, and a box from -180 to 180 encloses nothing. An edge along a pole, where every longitude meets, does not warn, so a cap around a pole closed along it does not either. If you meant the short way, region is what you drew. If you meant the long way, split the region into parts smaller than a hemisphere, add vertices to each as in the previous section, and pass the parts as a list; or switch to planar interpretation with sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE). Splitting works under the default setting. Switching has to happen before draw() and stay in force for every estimate from the sample; see the next section.

The s2 setting at draw time and after

Which rows fall inside region depends on sf::sf_use_s2(). With spherical geometry the edges of a longitude/latitude region are great-circle arcs, and without it they are straight lines in longitude and latitude, so rows near an edge can be inside under one setting and outside under the other. Use the same setting when you draw a sample and whenever you analyse it.

ht_total(), ht_mean(), as_svydesign() and sample_summary() find the region's rows again each time they run, because the variance, the design effect and survey's population count all depend on them. They compare the result with the inclusion probabilities stored at draw time, or with the .prob column of a sample saved by drawn 0.2.0, and refuse the sample when the two differ, naming sf::sf_use_s2(). The comparison catches any change in which rows are inside, including one that comes with another version of sf. A region that holds fewer than n rows under the current setting leaves nothing to compare, and the sample is refused the same way. The point estimate would not have moved, since it uses the stored .prob, but the standard error would.

sf_use_s2() is a session setting, and a new R session starts with it TRUE unless the _SF_USE_S2 environment variable says otherwise. A sample drawn under sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE) and saved with saveRDS() needs sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE) again after readRDS(). inclusion_prob() and joint_prob() on the frame follow the current setting too.

See also

draw()

Other designs: design_bootstrap(), design_certainty(), design_cluster(), design_multistage(), design_reservoir(), design_simple(), design_spread(), design_stratified(), design_systematic(), design_temporal(), design_weighted()

Examples

box <- sf::st_sfc(
  sf::st_polygon(list(cbind(c(0, 10, 10, 0, 0), c(0, 0, 10, 10, 0)))),
  crs = 4326
)
df <- data.frame(id = 1:20,
                 lon = seq(1, 9, length.out = 20),
                 lat = seq(1, 9, length.out = 20))
draw(df, design_spatial(c("lon", "lat"), region = box, n = 5), seed = 1)
#>   id      lon      lat
#> 1  1 1.000000 1.000000
#> 2  2 1.421053 1.421053
#> 3  4 2.263158 2.263158
#> 4  7 3.526316 3.526316
#> 5 13 6.052632 6.052632
